newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Labor Ready backs 1997 EPS view.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Labor Ready backs 1997 EPS view.

text.p: Labor Ready Inc expects to meet analysts' earnings estimates of $0.42-$0.44 a share on revenues of $300 million in fiscal 1997 as the number of paychecks the temporary manual labor provider processes nearly doubles.
"We're basically on track to meet analysts' estimates of $0.42 to $0.44 a share for 1997," said Ralph Peterson, chief operating officer of Labor Ready, in an interview Tuesday.
Peterson said he is comfortable with analyst's projections of revenue of $300 million for the year.
He said he expects the company to process 4.0 million paychecks in 1997 to its temporary workers, who get paid daily, up from the 2.1 million processed in 1996.

Labor Ready, which is headquartered in Tacoma, Washington, earned $724,000, or $0.06 a share, after a $1.2 million, or $0.11 extraordinary charge for the prepayment of debt, on revenues of $163.4 million for the fiscal year ended December 31, 1996.
The company earned $2.1 million, or $0.23 a share, on revenues of $94.4 million in 1995.

The company, which expects to grow rapidly through new stores, or dispatch locations, and through acquisitions, plans to add 100 locations a year for the "forseeable future" from its current base of 300. The company puts in most of its stores within the first six months of the year, to take advantage of the stronger spring, summer and early fall seasons.

"We expect to have 750 dispatch locations in the year 2001," stated Glenn Walstad, Labor Ready's president. "We expect to reach $1 billion in revenues in the year 2001 and to put five percent of that on the bottom line," he told Reuters.

"I think they are going to do well," said Ian Gilson of Van Kasper & Co. "The stock fell because they were unable to meet fourth quarter earnings and revenue projections, but since then, they have corrected that.
In April, Labor Ready reported a first quarter loss of $0.06 versus a loss of $0.08 the year before. The company's stock closed Monday at $9.87, having traded as high as 25 last September.
Gilson noted that with most this year's openings already complete, Labor Ready will benefit from higher revenues, with less of a penalty for opening stores the rest of the year.

The initial cost of adding a location has risen to $60,000 in 1996 from $35,000 in 1995 and $25,000 in 1994. The executives see costs continuing at $60,000 per unit in 1997, primarily due to increased training costs for internal personnel.
"Recently we have been putting more emphasis on training potential managers and customer service sales representatives," said Peterson.

Labor Ready began an intensive training program for its internal personnel in the autumn of 1996. Increased training expense primarily affected the second half of the year, but the company also boosted advertising expense and invested in hardware.
"A barrier to entry (for this business) is our systems," noted Peterson. "You can't get up and running without systems," he said.

Besides processing checks, the company's systems also allow rapid credit checks on potential clients, who get billed weekly. One percent of accounts receivables is reserved for bad debt and aging of receivables is 34 to 35 days, the executives said.
Walstad said the company projects cash flow to be sufficient for internal growth, but it may have to raise capital to make acquisitions.
He said that the company, which announced that it is seeking acquisitions in April, is in preliminary discussions with potential candidates in the same field.
